Matchup-Driven

Trey McBride is a genuine centerpiece, not an afterthought — 28% of targets (league ~15%).

The Offensive Blueprint

There's no bell-cow to bank on — the lead back sees just 49% of carries (league ~59%), a committee that caps any one back's ceiling and makes their rushing props matchup- and script-dependent.

This is an aggressive, pass-leaning attack: +1% pass rate over expected, top of the league's range, and no interest in sitting on a lead (45% pass when ahead).

When they fall behind they abandon the run entirely — 64% pass while trailing, so their pass-catchers have huge comeback-script ceilings.

In the Red Zone

Their red-zone identity is pass-first (59% pass), which puts scoring equity on Michael Wilson. And with the TE commanding 28% of targets, Trey McBride is a live red-zone option too.

Defense — Soft on the Ground

They surrender 128 rushing and 237 passing yards per game (league ~120 / ~230). The run moves against them — target opposing RB1s.

Soft against backs out of the backfield — 23 rec yds/game (vs ~18). A rec-yards target.

They lock down opposing WR2s — just 30 rec yds/game (vs ~36); fade receiving props there.

Broadly a leaky unit — 48% success rate allowed (vs ~44%); points come easy against them.

They leak WR1 receiving TDs (0.47/game vs ~0.38) — an anytime-TD spot to attack.

They leak TE touchdowns (0.32/game vs ~0.24) — an anytime-TD spot to attack.

The Betting Angles

Bottom line: their pass-catchers have massive ceilings in comeback scripts (fade-material as underdogs); opposing RB1s smash on the ground and at the goal line; opposing TE anytime-TD is a repeatable angle.

Built on 2024–25 data; the profile rebuilds through the season as the current staff and roster set their own tendencies.
